doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Sitting in with rock and blues bands as a teenager
summary: Fleetwood Mac, Mayall and Hendrix played small rooms; he asked to sit in, played within himself, and built contacts while on a university grant.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I was curious, there’s anecdotes that you’ve shared about, probably not that long after that, sitting in with some of the now-well-known rock bands. You’d go to a club and, did you have to like make your way through the bouncers and the manager or whatever?

No the interesting thing is there weren’t any in those days, and we’re talking about, you know, bands like Fleetwood Mac and John Mayall’s Bluesbreakers and even the Jimi Hendrix Experience would be playing in local bars, you know, in the back room or upstairs. There were no dressing rooms let alone bouncers. And you’d see someone at the bar and you’d take your tenor along, or I’d take my tenor along, and I’d say, “Can I play with you?” And quite usually they would say yeah, sure. And it wasn’t a case of well we know who you are so come and join us. It was more a case of well we’ll give you one tune and if you’re no good we’ll kick you off. And if you can play we’ll ask you to stay for the whole evening. And once you got to know them you’d play maybe one solo or something and they went, “Oh this guy’s all right.” At the end of the evening they’d say we’re playing another club next Saturday, why don’t you join us — or I’ve got another band, come and play with them, or my friend’s band is so-and-so, tell them that you played with us and join in. So I built up this whole circle of jamming and I always say I was very lucky because I went to University on a full grant. So I didn’t need to turn professional, I could go and jam with whoever I felt like and it wasn’t an economic necessity to go on tour with a soul band or play in a holiday camp for the whole summer. I would show up at gigs or even at University, my roommate was social secretary so I got him to book all the people I could play with.
Nice deal. When you got up on the stage, would they usually call one of their originals or would they do like a blues or something?

It would be a blues mainly, yes. And then you basically would be in that position where I mean obviously a lot of people would get up and they would try and show off, because they would go oh I’ve got two choruses to show that I’m a genius. You know? I never had that feeling. I always felt well I’ve got to fit in and contribute to what they’re doing. Therefore I’m going to play, you know, within myself but make it musical and make it make sense. I always had that notion in my head, that I would do that rather than, you know, show off or do something technical that people’d go wow, he’s technically good.
Yeah. Or cover up a singer.

Oh yeah, no that was the other thing. I mean I was actually on one gig where the singer turned to me and said, “Can you please go and shut that other guy up?” He won’t stop playing you know. So I was very lucky I think you know, to build up that series of contacts before I actually knew that I was going to go professional.
